Setting up a home NAS (Network Attached Storage) is a great way to build your own private cloud for file storage, backups, media streaming, and remote access.

There are three main approaches, depending on your budget and how much control you want.

1. Choose your NAS setup

Option A: Prebuilt NAS — easiest

Synology or QNAP

Simple web interface, automated backups, file sharing, and mobile apps.

Approx. $250–$700+ without drives

Option B: Mini PC NAS — flexible

Intel N100/N150 mini PC running OpenMediaVault or TrueNAS.

Good for Docker, Plex, backups, and experimenting with self-hosted services.

Approx. $200–$500+ without drives

Option C: Custom-built NAS — maximum control

Build a dedicated server with multiple HDDs, TrueNAS SCALE, and optional 2.5/10GbE networking.

Best for large storage pools, virtualization, and expansion.

Approx. $400–$1,000+ without drives

For a typical home NAS, I'd start with two or four drive bays, wired Ethernet, mirrored drives for availability, and a separate backup. RAID is not a backup. For remote access, use a VPN such as Tailscale rather than exposing NAS management ports directly to the internet.

Setting up a home NAS (Network Attached Storage) is a great way to create your own private cloud for file storage, backups, media streaming, and remote access.

There are three main approaches, depending on your budget and how much control you want.

1. Choose your NAS setup

Option A: Prebuilt NAS — easiest

Synology or QNAP

Estimated cost: $250–$600+ without drives.

Simple setup, polished software, automatic backups, remote access.

Option B: DIY NAS — most flexible

Mini PC or custom PC running TrueNAS or Unraid.

Estimated cost: $200–$700+ without drives.

Great for Docker, Plex, home servers, and expandable storage.

Option C: Mini PC + external storage — budget

Estimated cost: $150–$350+ without drives.

Low power consumption and compact, but USB-attached drives are less ideal for robust multi-disk NAS arrays.

2. Recommended home NAS architecture

For a typical home, I'd recommend:

NAS: 4-bay enclosure for future expansion

Drives: 2 × 8 TB NAS-rated HDDs to start

Redundancy: RAID 1 or equivalent mirror (8 TB usable before formatting and filesystem overhead)

Network: 2.5 GbE if supported by your equipment

Access: SMB for Windows/macOS, Tailscale for secure remote access

Backups: External drive or cloud backup, because RAID is not a backup

If you're looking for a NAS (Network Attached Storage) for Plex Media Server, the most important factor is whether you need hardware transcoding or just direct playback.

Best NAS options for Plex

Synology DS224+

Best for simplicity. Intel CPU with Quick Sync hardware transcoding, 2 drive bays, and an easy-to-use operating system.

QNAP TS-464

Best for flexibility. Intel Celeron N5095, 4 drive bays, 2.5GbE networking, and good Plex hardware transcoding support.

UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus

Best for performance. Intel Pentium Gold 8505 with Quick Sync, 4 drive bays, and 10GbE connectivity.

What matters for Plex

Intel Quick Sync: Highly recommended for transcoding, especially 4K video.

Plex Pass: Hardware-accelerated transcoding generally requires Plex Pass.

RAM: 4–8 GB is sufficient for most Plex setups.

Storage: 4 bays are preferable if you plan to grow your media library.

Direct Play: If all clients support your video formats, even a low-powered NAS can work well.

If you're looking for a NAS (Network Attached Storage) for Plex Media Server, the most important factors are hardware transcoding support, CPU performance, storage capacity, and price.
